conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time for this today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health specialist. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.

To get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to run through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, ten-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and thoughts that can pop up in the first months after birth. Anything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise—or unless I feel you might be in immediate danger, in which case I’d talk with you first about next steps.

We’ll go one question at a time, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you over the past seven days. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve mostly kept my sense of humor—my partner and I still chuckled at a silly meme yesterday—but I notice I don’t laugh as easily as I did before the baby. There are moments when something strikes me as funny, but it feels a bit muted, like I’m enjoying it less than I know I used to. So I’d say I can still laugh, just not quite with the same spark.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh—maybe not quite as heartily as before, but I do find things funny sometimes. It just feels a little more muted lately.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom brings dinner or when I get to take a quiet shower—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the hours like I did before the baby came.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

A couple of times this week I caught myself thinking, “If I were better at this, she wouldn’t have cried for so long,” or “I should’ve known to change her diaper sooner.” I know rationally it’s not really my fault, but those thoughts still pop up and make me feel sort of inadequate for a little while.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday, the baby sneezed twice and my mind jumped straight to “What if she’s getting really sick?” even though she was fine and had no fever. I calmed down pretty quickly, but the worry came out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just a quick rush of “what-if” when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., but it passed once I rocked her back to sleep.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she cluster-fed and wouldn’t nap yesterday, I felt like the dishes, laundry, and texts from friends were all piling up and I couldn’t catch my breath. I managed, but it felt heavier than usual—like I was one step away from dropping something.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve still been able to sleep okay. Once I finally lie down, I drift off pretty quickly—unless she needs me, of course.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a few moments—mostly in the late afternoon when I’m tired—where I just feel kind of blue and teary, but it lifts after a little while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when my partner found me folding laundry at midnight. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that stopped after a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wks post-delivery  
Source: self-report EPDS-style questionnaire  

<sym>Endorsed symptoms / concerns</sym>  
- Anhedonia: “muted” laughter, anticipatory pleasure reduced  
- Mild depressive dips: late-afternoon tearfulness, transient crying when overwhelmed  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“If I were better…”)  
- Episodic “what-if” worries and brief physiological surges (3 a.m. cannot-settle)  
- Feeling “one step away from dropping something” during cluster-care days  
- No sleep-onset problems unless infant needs; no self-harm ideation  

<sym>Pattern</sym>: sub-syndromal mood distress with prominent anxiety cognitions; functioning maintained but effort increased.

<med>Screening significance</med>  
Elevated risk for minor-moderate postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; not meeting high-risk threshold for self-harm or melancholic depression at present.

<sym>Risk factors noted</sym>  
- Frequent self-critical attributions  
- Situational tearfulness >2×/week  
- Perceived coping strain despite external support

Plan: Continue routine care; repeat standardized screening (EPDS) in 1–2 weeks or sooner if distress escalates, crying spells increase, or any new self-harm thoughts emerge.
